section_summary: The section opens with the end of a report on Japan’s raw materials, occupation army, emperor, and political development. Diplomatic reports then examine General Headquarters’ intervention in Japanese politics, a reported Hokkaido independence movement, press rights during elections, and the January 1949 general election. The final pages introduce a request for Korea to return two fugitives wanted by Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Report on Japan’s raw materials, occupation army, emperor, and politics
subfiles.about: A report assesses occupation policy and recommends changes to Japan’s economic, security, imperial, and political arrangements.
subfiles.summary: The report urges rehabilitation of coal mines and development of regional raw materials. It recommends narrowing the occupation army’s civilian role, creating a Japanese constabulary, and leaving the emperor’s constitutional position to the Japanese. Its political analysis criticizes SCAP intervention and the purge, warns of Communist gains, and favors lighter Allied oversight.

subfiles.title: General Headquarters Intervention in Japanese Politics
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The Political Adviser reports Japanese criticism of SCAP intervention in parliamentary affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ichimada and Ishikawa say Headquarters’ shifting positions on wages, legislation, and elections undermine the Yoshida cabinet and parliamentary government. The mission warns that weakening conservatives while the socialist center disintegrates could strengthen a Communist led opposition.

subfiles.title: General Headquarters Intervention in Japanese Politics
subfiles.about: Ichimada discusses Japan’s economic outlook and criticizes Headquarters’ handling of parliamentary decisions.
subfiles.summary: At a dinner with Spinks, Ichimada and Ishikawa discuss economic stabilization and possible trade with Communist China. Ichimada then describes Headquarters’ reversal over the base wage and interventions in Diet affairs, arguing that inconsistent outside pressure damages responsible government and Yoshida’s authority.

subfiles.title: Hokkaido Independence Movement
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The mission forwards an unverified account of Communist support for Hokkaido independence.
subfiles.summary: Mitamura claims Communists link Hokkaido independence to economic relief, fishing rights, and possible acquisition of the Kurils and Sakhalin. The mission notes evidence of a small independence movement but cannot verify his claims or Soviet backing.

subfiles.title: Hokkaido Independence Movement
subfiles.about: Mitamura recounts his survey of Communist organization and independence sentiment in Hokkaido.
subfiles.summary: Mitamura attributes Communist organizing strength to Hokkaido’s frontier character, economic stagnation, and party efforts. He says Communists quietly support independence and suggest that a people’s republic could gain the Kurils, Sakhalin, and Soviet fishing rights.

subfiles.title: New China News Agency commentary on Japanese elections and China
subfiles.about: The embassy relays a Chinese Communist radio commentary urging Japanese voters to support democratic candidates.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast condemns Japanese and American imperialism, anticipates relations between Japan and a Communist led China, and calls for friendship with Japanese democratic groups. It argues that the election is constrained by reactionary influence but urges voters to elect more democratic representatives.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Prerogatives in Elections
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The adviser forwards materials resolving whether newspapers may endorse election candidates.
subfiles.summary: Three enclosures document official acceptance of newspaper commentary on candidates.

subfiles.title: Law Concerning the Provisional Exceptions to Election Campaigns and Others, Articles 18–21
subfiles.about: A translated election law regulates campaign advertisements, printed material, signs, and candidate endorsements.
subfiles.summary: The provisions permit limited newspaper advertisements while restricting campaign writings and displays. Article 21 bars material chiefly endorsing or opposing candidates when used to evade those restrictions.

subfiles.title: Statement by Major Daniel C. Imboden on newspaper election commentary
subfiles.about: A SCAP press official says newspapers may support or criticize parties and candidates.
subfiles.summary: Imboden invokes constitutional press freedom and urges newspapers to assess candidates, parties, and election issues openly.

subfiles.title: Announcement on press reporting in the election
subfiles.about: The commission calls for fair, active newspaper criticism of parties and candidates.
subfiles.summary: The commission affirms press freedom and urges responsible election coverage.

subfiles.title: Embassy assessment of North Shensi broadcast on Japanese elections
subfiles.about: The embassy interprets Chinese Communist interest in Japan’s election and future trade.
subfiles.summary: It sees concern over a democratic Japan and interest in economic exchange with Japan.

subfiles.title: Soviet press commentary on Japanese elections
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Soviet press criticism of occupation election policy.
subfiles.summary: Soviet papers allege repression of Japanese Communists and manipulation of the election.

subfiles.title: Possible Reasons for Communist Successes in January 23, 1949
subfiles.about: A memorandum lists possible causes of Communist electoral gains.
subfiles.summary: It cites the party’s broader platform, labor organizing, scandals, foreign capital policy, and Chinese Communist victories.

subfiles.title: Transmitting text of United Press Interview with Premier Yoshida
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The adviser forwards Yoshida’s interview and press accounts of a proposed purge appeals committee.
subfiles.summary: The despatch compares Yoshida’s proposal to review potentially unjust purges with SCAP’s denial of any general purge amnesty. It encloses the interview and three related press items.

subfiles.title: United Press interview with Premier Yoshida
subfiles.about: Yoshida discusses economic reconstruction, purge appeals, China, elections, and Communist infiltration.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida promises reconstruction committees and an appeals board for disputed purges, and expects electoral success.

subfiles.title: Purge Amnesty Is Not Planned
subfiles.about: A SCAP officer denies reports that purge categories will be relaxed.
subfiles.summary: Major Napier says SCAP is considering no change to existing purge definitions.

subfiles.title: Definite Plan for Purge Review Committee Completed
subfiles.about: A newspaper reports preparations for a committee to hear purge appeals.
subfiles.summary: The proposed committee would clear only people whose purges were plainly unjustified.

subfiles.title: On the Purge
subfiles.about: An editorial weighs the benefits and difficulties of readmitting purged officials.
subfiles.summary: It supports useful personnel returning but prefers new political leaders.

subfiles.title: Japanese general election results, A-16
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The first election airgram considers how electoral rules helped the Communist Party win seats.
subfiles.summary: It argues that concentrating one Communist candidate in each district favored a disciplined minority party while larger parties divided their vote among several candidates.

subfiles.title: Japanese general election results, A-17
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The second election airgram reviews party results and the decline of the socialist center.
subfiles.summary: It reports a large Democratic Liberal victory, Social Democratic losses, and Communist gains. The adviser expects Yoshida to form a single party cabinet and warns that Communist leaders may claim leadership of the opposition.

subfiles.title: Japanese general election assessment, A-18
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The adviser interprets the conservative victory and Communist gains.
subfiles.summary: The airgram cautions that many voters chose Yoshida’s party because moderate parties offered little alternative, rather than from hostility to the Occupation. It urges attention to Communist strength and rebuilding a credible political center.

subfiles.title: MacArthur’s statistical summary and analysis of the January 1949 general election
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The telegram transmits MacArthur’s official election figures and political analysis.
subfiles.summary: The report tabulates population, voters, candidates, turnout, seats, new members, women elected, and prominent defeated candidates. It records 264 seats for the Democratic Liberals and 35 for the Communists. Its analysis links conservative success to a campaign for stable government and Communist gains to socialist losses, Chinese events, and protest votes.

subfiles.title: Soviet press reaction to Japanese election results
subfiles.about: The embassy summarizes Soviet praise for Communist electoral gains.
subfiles.summary: Soviet papers portray the Communist result as a blow to Japanese reaction.

subfiles.title: Chinese press reaction to Japanese election results
subfiles.about: The consulate summarizes Chinese newspaper views of Communist gains and political polarization in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorials link Communist gains to events in China and note the weakening of Japan’s political center.

subfiles.title: French press assessment of Japanese general election
subfiles.about: The embassy reports French commentary on Japan’s conservative victory, moderate losses, and Communist progress.
subfiles.summary: The commentary expects the Liberal majority to bring political stability while suggesting Yoshida may bargain more firmly with the Occupation. It treats the result as a shift to the right without assuming a return to prewar militarism.

subfiles.title: Transmission of note to Korea requesting rendition of two fugitives
subfiles.about: The mission forwards its note asking Korea to return two men wanted in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The request rests on comity because no extradition treaty applies.

subfiles.title: Note requesting apprehension and rendition of Lee Kil Moon and Kang Yong Soo
subfiles.to: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea
subfiles.about: The mission requests Korea’s help returning two fugitives accused of fraud in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Lee and Kang, gives possible locations and descriptions, and outlines allegations that they helped forge checks and smuggle proceeds into Korea. It acknowledges that Korea has no treaty duty to extradite them, requests cooperation on grounds of comity, and lists supporting letters.
